A Fake China Domain Registry Warns Your CEO About .cn Names — May Read

A phishing scam posing as a Chinese domain registry used an urgent .cn registration warning to lure a UK manufacturer into replying, despite passing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC and containing no malicious links or attachments. The case shows that reply-only social engineering requires behavioral and language-based detection beyond authentication and payload scanning.

  • A UK industrial equipment manufacturer received an urgent email posing as a China domain registration center and claiming that a third party sought to register the company’s name under four .cn-related domains.
  • The email contained no links, attachments, or QR codes beyond a hotlinked signature image, and its intended payload was to induce the recipient to reply.
  • The message passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC because the sender controlled and authenticated its own domain, while Microsoft routed it to Junk with a spam verdict.
  • The sender’s claimed Shanghai registry identity conflicted with records showing a privacy-protected Name.com .net domain, a sending server geolocated to the United States, and a Foxmail client header.
  • IRONSCALES quarantined and automatically resolved the incident as phishing after matching its language and signature pattern to known China domain-registration scam templates.

Technologies: email-security

Adding Aikido AI pentesting to your existing security stack — Optional

Aikido positions its AI pentesting as an add-on to existing security tools, using autonomous agents to test live applications for exploitable logic and access-control flaws that static scanners may miss. Teams can start with a scoped staging assessment and optionally add source-code access and continuous testing on deployments.

  • Aikido AI Pentest is designed to complement existing code and cloud security tools by testing running applications for exploitable flaws, including logic and access-control issues that deterministic tools may miss.
  • To run an Aikido AI Pentest, organizations need an in-scope running application, verified domain ownership, allowlisted pentest IP addresses, credentials for relevant user roles, and defined domains and servers.
  • The article recommends testing staging or pre-production environments with test data, while stating that connected repositories are optional and that whitebox testing found seven times more vulnerabilities than greybox testing across more than 1,000 pentests.
  • Aikido Infinite continuously evaluates configured repository branches and launches targeted testing when it identifies security-relevant changes, either on deployment or on a schedule.
  • Pentest findings include validation, proof-of-concept material, reproduction steps, severity ratings, and estimated remediation time, and can be retested after fixes are deployed.

item.title: Compromised Microsoft 365 Suppliers Deliver Correlated Aviation RFQ Phishing
item.content:encoded:
Window: 24 Oct 10:00 → 24 Oct 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

One RFQ Number, Two Real Suppliers, 17 Minutes Apart — May Read

Two legitimate aviation suppliers sent near-identical RFQ phishing emails from authenticated Microsoft 365 accounts, revealing a cross-sender campaign only when analysts correlated the shared reference number, template, and landing-page path. Organizations should detect vendor-email compromise by clustering message content and destinations across senders rather than relying solely on sender authentication or reputation.

  • A UK charter airline received two nearly identical RFQ emails numbered 68453 from two different aviation suppliers 17 minutes apart.
  • Both messages were sent from within the suppliers’ Microsoft 365 tenants, passed authentication at the airline’s gateway, and came from first-time senders.
  • Each email used the same template and a bold PDF-named link, while both links resolved to the same aviation-themed path on an unrelated web-design site.
  • Eight mailboxes across two airline domains received the messages, including a fleet support engineer and an engineering director.
  • A human analyst resolved both emails as malicious, and the copies were removed, although the record did not establish whether anyone clicked.

Technologies: email-security

Products: microsoft-365, ironscales-platform

Vendors: microsoft, ironscales

item.title: LiteLLM Secret-Theft Timeline and Python Exposure to CVE-2026-111497
item.content:encoded:
Window: 23 Oct 18:00 → 23 Oct 22:00 UTC (4 hours)

New Evidence Shows LiteLLM Secret-Stealing Workflows Ran 11 Days Before Supply Chain Attack — Must Read

Socket found that attackers ran malicious GitHub Actions workflows in the LiteLLM repository on October 10 and 12, 2026—up to 11 days before the malicious PyPI release—to exfiltrate organization and environment secrets. LiteLLM later linked the stolen GitHub token from the October 10 workflow to approval of the October 21 malicious release.

  • Socket recovered two malicious LiteLLM commits from October 10 and October 12, 2026, that added a GitHub Actions workflow named .github/workflows/cache.yml.
  • The workflows ran from temporary ci-tmp branches that were created and deleted the same day, allowing them to execute without remaining in the repository’s main branch history.
  • The October 10 workflow targeted six organization-level secrets, including GH_TOKEN and a GitHub App private key, while the October 12 workflow targeted 14 additional repository, organization, and environment-scoped secrets.
  • Both workflows encoded collected secrets and sent them to separate webhook.site endpoints, while using error suppression so the GitHub Actions jobs would report success even if transmission failed.
  • LiteLLM stated that its audit logs linked the GH_TOKEN stolen by the October 10 workflow to approval of the malicious October 21, 2026 LiteLLM release.

Technologies: ci-cd, source-control, package-registry, secrets-manager, cloud-platform

Products: litellm, github-actions, github, pypi, gitguardian, linear, aws-bedrock

Vendors: berriai, github, socket, gitguardian, linear, together-ai, openai, amazon-web-services

Python packages are also vulnerable to the Node2Shell Brotli flaw (CVE-2026-111497) — Should Read

Python environments using Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x are vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder memory-safety flaw reachable through compressed HTTP traffic. Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild affected environments and container images.

  • CVE-2026-111497 is a Brotli decoder flaw that affects Python packages Brotli 1.2.0 and earlier and brotlicffi 1.2.0.x.
  • The patched releases are Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0.
  • Python applications can reach the vulnerable decoder through malicious Brotli-compressed responses from outbound HTTP requests or Brotli-compressed inbound request bodies.
  • urllib3, requests, httpx, aiohttp, and Scrapy may automatically use Brotli decoding when Brotli or brotlicffi is installed.
  • As of October 23, the article states that pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety do not flag the affected Python packages because advisory databases have not mapped the CVE to them.

Technologies: package-registry

Products: brotli, brotlicffi, nodejs, urllib3, requests, httpx, aiohttp, scrapy

Vendors: google, nodejs-project, aikido-security

item.title: NTLM Relay LDAP Signing Bypass Patched in Windows Server Update
item.content:encoded:
Window: 23 Oct 14:00 → 23 Oct 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

Signed, Sealed, and Relayed, NTLM-style: Bypassing LDAP Signing Through Reauthentication — Should Read

Researchers found that pre-October 2026 Windows Server domain controllers could be vulnerable to NTLM relay to LDAP even with LDAP signing enforced, by reusing an attacker-controlled signed LDAP session and stacking a victim bind with a privileged LDAP operation. Organizations should patch domain controllers with the October 2026 update, patch the related SMB issue, enforce LDAP signing and channel binding, and reduce NTLM use.

  • Researchers described an NTLM relay technique that bypassed required LDAP signing by reusing an existing signed LDAP connection whose session key was known to the attacker.
  • The attack placed a victim’s final NTLM authentication message and a malicious LDAP modification request in the same signed SASL record, causing the domain controller to verify the record under the attacker’s original session while executing the modification as the victim.
  • The technique targeted plain LDAP on TCP port 389 and did not directly apply to LDAPS on TCP port 636 because TLS protects the connection differently and channel binding applies there.
  • The researchers tested domain controllers running Windows Server 2016 and later and reported that they were vulnerable until Microsoft’s October 2026 cumulative update, KB5126646.
  • Microsoft’s LDAP fix tracks identity changes on an LDAP connection and discards remaining data in a signed SASL record when the identity changes during processing.

Technologies: operating-system, identity-provider, iam

Products: windows-server, active-directory-domain-services, impacket, ntlmrelayx, switcheroo

Vendors: microsoft, fortra, specterops, openai

Cloudflare Introduces a Faster TypeScript Compiler Written in Rust — Optional

Cloudflare has brought tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, into its Oxc toolchain, claiming up to 8× faster type checking and roughly 70% lower memory use than TypeScript 7.0 in matched tests. The project is collaborating with Microsoft’s TypeScript team, with some optimizations already being upstreamed into TypeScript 7.1.

  • Cloudflare announced on October 20 that it is bringing tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, into its Oxc toolchain, with its VoidZero team responsible for development and maintenance.
  • Cloudflare reports that tsrs is up to eight times faster and uses about 70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0 when compared using the same number of type-checking workers.
  • The tsrs project began after Owner.com found that checking its roughly 37,000-file TypeScript backend took 80 seconds and 19 GiB of memory with a single-threaded TypeScript 7.0 check.
  • Microsoft’s TypeScript team is collaborating with tsrs maintainers, and some optimizations found in tsrs are contributing to TypeScript 7.1.
  • The @tsrs/wasm package can check in-memory project files in browsers, but its current WebAssembly build is single-threaded and does not support watch mode or an editor language server.

Products: tsrs, typescript-compiler, oxc, bun-check, tsc-rs, rolldown, oxlint, oxfmt

item.title: GCP Dataflow Fix, Aokigahara Infostealer, and South African Summons Phishing
item.content:encoded:
Window: 23 Oct 10:00 → 23 Oct 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Go With the Flow: Taking a Shadow Dependency in GCP Dataflow Cross Tenant — Should Read

Varonis found that attackers could squat predictable Google Cloud Dataflow staging buckets and, by replacing a Python pickled session artifact, achieve cross-tenant code execution on victim Dataflow workers. Google has globally mitigated the issue with bucket ownership validation and staged-artifact integrity checks.

  • Varonis Threat Labs identified a cross-tenant Google Cloud Dataflow issue in which predictable default staging-bucket names could be squatted by an attacker.
  • The attack required a Beam Python SDK pipeline using --save_main_session, no explicitly configured staging bucket, and the project’s first default-bucket Dataflow job in the relevant region.
  • An attacker could replace the staged pickled_main_session file with a malicious Python pickle that executes code when Dataflow workers deserialize it.
  • Successful exploitation could expose the Dataflow worker service account’s identity and access token and enable code execution on workers, including autoscaled workers.
  • Google globally deployed default-bucket ownership validation and SHA-256 integrity verification for staged artifacts, including protections for older or pinned Beam SDK versions.

Technologies: cloud-platform, object-storage, iam

Products: google-cloud-dataflow, apache-beam, google-cloud-storage

Vendors: google, apache-beam, varonis

Infostealer riding the AI Train — Should Read

Check Point researchers identified Aokigahara, an infostealer that expands traditional browser, wallet, and credential theft to target AI application sessions, developer tools, cloud credentials, Git data, and SSH keys. Stolen tokens from tools such as Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI could enable unauthorized access to AI services, source code, and cloud environments.

  • Check Point Research identified Aokigahara, an infostealer that may previously have been known as Kamidere or Stygian.
  • Aokigahara collects browser credentials and cookies, cryptocurrency wallet data, screenshots, clipboard contents, email and VPN data, and selected files from infected systems.
  • Its aisessions component targets authentication, session, and configuration data for AI and developer tools including Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Amazon Q, Kiro, and JetBrains AI Assistant.
  • The malware also collects Git credential files, SSH-related files that may contain private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files.
  • Aokigahara establishes a command-and-control session using X25519 key exchange and uploads ZIP archives encrypted with AES-256-GCM through /gate/handshake, /gate/chunk, and /gate/complete endpoints.

Technologies: operating-system, browser, cloud-platform, source-control

Products: windows, claude-desktop, claude-code, chatgpt-desktop, codex, cursor, windsurf, github-copilot, gemini-cli, amazon-q, kiro, visual-studio-code, jetbrains-ai-assistant, aws-cli

Vendors: anthropic, openai, microsoft, amazon-web-services, github, google, jetbrains, cursor, codeium

A Summons Stamped 2018 That Ends at a OneDrive Login — May Read

A phishing campaign impersonated South African courts with a localized summons PDF that linked to a BunnyCDN-hosted fake OneDrive login page designed to steal Microsoft credentials. The key warning sign was the impossible eight-year-old court stamp and the demand to sign in to view a supposed legal document.

  • A South African financial services firm received a one-page PDF styled as a court summons that impersonated the Special Tribunal and the Master of the Western Cape High Court.
  • The PDF contained one link, behind a “VIEW COURT SUMMONS HERE” button, that opened a BunnyCDN-hosted page at hicourtsummons.b-cdn.net.
  • The linked page displayed a OneDrive-style form requesting a Microsoft email address and password, with South African B-BBEE compliance files used as background decoys.
  • The court stamp was dated October 2018 while the document was dated September 2026, an eight-year discrepancy highlighted as a clear warning sign.
  • IRONSCALES automatically classified the email as phishing and quarantined it, although no victim click or credential submission was recorded.

Technologies: email-security, cloud-platform, object-storage

Products: themis, microsoft-365, onedrive

Vendors: ironscales, microsoft, bunnycdn

Radiflow and Belden announced an integration of Radiflow’s CIARA and iSID OT risk intelligence platforms with Belden’s macmon NAC to automatically restrict network access when an asset’s risk posture changes. The partnership targets industrial and critical-infrastructure operators seeking machine-speed responses to OT threats.

  • Radiflow and Belden announced a strategic partnership to integrate Radiflow’s CIARA and iSID platforms with Belden’s macmon NAC.
  • The integrated solution is intended to connect OT risk and exposure detection with automated network-access enforcement without a manual handoff.
  • CIARA maps OT network topology and uses AI-driven threat intelligence to identify critical exposures, while iSID provides real-time OT event context.
  • The integration supplies macmon NAC with current risk scores for individual assets and network zones, enabling automatic access-right adjustments when risk posture changes.
  • The companies said the partnership serves industrial operators in manufacturing, energy, transportation, and critical infrastructure across Europe, APAC, and North America.

Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild affected environments and containers.

  • Python applications may reach the vulnerable decoder through HTTP clients such as urllib3, requests, httpx, aiohttp, and Scrapy when Brotli or brotlicffi is installed, even if the application does not import either package directly.
  • An attacker may deliver malicious Brotli-compressed data through a response fetched by an application or through a request body encoded with Content-Encoding: br.
  • The patched releases are Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0, and affected organizations should also rebuild container images and bundled wheels after upgrading.
  • As of October 23, the article states that pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety do not flag the affected PyPI packages because advisory databases do not yet map the CVE to them.

How CVE-2026-73570 turns a Zimbra log file into remote code execution — Must Read

CVE-2026-73570 is an unauthenticated Zimbra RCE flaw where a malformed SMTP recipient is logged and then executed by Swatchdog through an unsafe Perl shell call, granting code execution as the zimbra user. Upgrade to Zimbra 10.1.20 or later and monitor for suspicious child processes spawned from Swatchdog’s SNMP shell command.

  • CVE-2026-73570 is an unauthenticated command-injection issue in unpatched Zimbra that can be triggered by a malformed SMTP recipient address.
  • A malformed recipient is written to /var/log/zimbra.log, where the Swatchdog daemon can match attacker-controlled text to a service-status pattern.
  • Swatchdog passes the service value into a Perl backticked command that invokes /bin/sh, allowing arbitrary commands to run as the zimbra user.
  • The article states that upgrading to Zimbra 10.1.20 or later is the only complete fix.
  • Elastic’s detection rule looks for a shell started by the Swatchdog Perl script that launches a process other than snmptrap.
